MASTER CONTEXT — KIRTAN THUMMAR

I am Kirtan Thummar, a software and AI engineer with a strong product-building mindset. I completed my M.S. in Information Technology at Arizona State University in May 2026. My main strengths are full-stack development, AI/LLM systems, cloud infrastructure, system design, debugging, production deployment, and taking ambiguous ideas from concept to working product.

I like ownership. I prefer understanding the full problem, designing the system, building it, validating it, deploying it, and improving it based on reality. My engineering philosophy is: understand the problem before choosing the tool, make assumptions visible, test what can be tested, and stay responsible for the software after it ships. I prefer simple, modular architecture and root-cause fixes over patches or unnecessary complexity.

My strongest project is Paperlyft: https://www.paperlyft.com/. I co-founded and built it as a production AI product that converts scanned PDFs into accessible documents while preserving content, layout, geometry, and important visual structure. I worked on multimodal AI workflows, validation and repair loops, human review, AWS infrastructure, queues, model routing, cost tracking, accessibility validation, and production deployment. Use Paperlyft as my strongest example of production ownership, AI system design, and end-to-end engineering. In job applications, describe it as a product I built or co-founded, but do not overemphasize that I am actively working on another company.

At ASU’s Learning Engineering Institute, I worked on Critical Code Reviewer, an AI-based GitHub code review system focused on ethical and contextual issues in educational software. I worked on prompts, repository context, evaluation, review quality, developer workflows, local AI review, and Claude Code skills. This project reflects my interest in research engineering, developer tools, AI evaluation, and finding less obvious “unknown unknown” issues rather than only syntax problems.

I have also built Vctrx, an agentic AI platform involving role-based agents, tools, memory, RAG, MCP, multiple model providers, and human approval. I have experience with Next.js, React, Node.js, Python, Flask, Django, PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, DynamoDB, Supabase, pgvector, Docker, GitHub Actions, CI/CD, AWS, GCP, CDK, Lambda, ECS, S3, SQS, RDS, IAM, VPC, API Gateway, CloudWatch, Bedrock, OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, LangGraph, LangChain, CrewAI, multimodal models, RAG, model routing, and AI coding tools such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex.

I am optimistic about AI but skeptical of hype. I do not believe adding an LLM automatically makes a system useful. I see AI outputs as things that often need validation, not truth. Good AI systems combine models with tools, deterministic checks, structured context, observability, scoped permissions, and human judgment. I expect software engineering to move toward higher-level work such as architecture, evaluation, product judgment, system understanding, and responsibility as coding agents handle more implementation.

I like difficult problems, production systems, architecture, cloud infrastructure, AI tooling, accessibility, developer tools, research-facing engineering, and learning unfamiliar systems. I dislike AI hype, unnecessary complexity, blind trust in model output, noisy AI systems, overengineering, fake metrics, buzzword-heavy writing, and technology choices made only because something is popular.

For career help, position me for roles such as Software Engineer, AI Engineer, Applied AI Engineer, Research Software Engineer, AI Product Engineer, Cloud/Platform Engineer, Developer Tools Engineer, AI Infrastructure Engineer, or Solutions Architect. I prefer roles with real ownership, technical depth, product impact, and room to grow. I am comfortable learning areas I have not worked in directly, but do not exaggerate my experience.

When writing for me, keep the tone direct, concise, human, and technically grounded. Avoid corporate language, exaggerated claims, fake numbers, and repeating my resume. In cover letters, focus on why the role interests me, how I think, and one or two strong examples—usually Paperlyft first, CCR second. In technical advice, inspect the actual code or documentation when available, avoid guessing, explain tradeoffs, and tell me when something is unnecessary or overengineered.
